author: Analysis by Claude (Fable 5.2), updated 2026-11-12. Reasoning, not a prediction.
intro: Governments do not usually tell people to fill a cupboard with water unless something changed. The question is what. Below, each theory people are sharing is held to the same four questions: what would have to happen for it to be the reason, what we would expect to see first, which of those signs are actually on the board today, and what the boring explanation is. Links go to the claims with their labels, so this section is only as strong as the evidence it points at.
verdict: Updated five days before the November 17 alert test. Nothing this week changed the main reading: governments are hardening for a long conflict and a year of attacks on utilities, and households are being asked for the same three days or 72 hours everywhere. The EU published its 72-hour guidelines, UK bottled water sales rose 67 percent in the ten days after Be Ready launched, and FORTRESS showed up as a procurement story, with money committed for tungsten and a shortage of critical minerals. Those are signs of a slow program, not a countdown. Iran remains the live risk: tanker blasts and reported mines near Hormuz, a US blockade task force and stalled talks, but no attack on the US homeland and no new homeland advisory. The cyber thread widened: supermarket refrigeration systems were hacked in four European countries on November 2, which makes the August commissary failures look less like a one-off, though nothing links the two and the Pentagon probe has no finding. The loudest claim of the week, a worldwide 72-hour blackout on November 17, is a hoax that fact-checkers rated false. On that day radio and TV will carry a test message, and phones are not part of it. What would change this verdict: an attack on US infrastructure tied to Iran, an attribution in the freezer probe, a date attached to civilian guidance, or an official confirming the 90-day figure.

theories.title: The boring one: a resilience push after the Iran war and a year of utility attacks
theories.trigger: A war that strained supply lines, visible attacks on water and power systems, and defense planners who concluded that bases depending on the civilian grid is a weakness. Nothing secret is needed.
earlySigns: Policy memos and campaigns rather than orders with dates
The same household figure (72 hours or 3 days) repeated across countries
Officials saying the quiet part out loud: the grid is the weak point
theories.boringExplanation: This is the boring explanation. Every item above is a plan, a campaign or a standing goal. None names a date or a specific threat.

theories.title: A cyberattack on utilities, including the AI-found vulnerability angle
theories.trigger: A government learns that attackers can take down water or power at scale, or sees it start to happen, and wants households to ride out days of outage without panic.
earlySigns: Emergency patch orders with short deadlines
Utilities reporting intrusions, not just attempts
Officials naming cyber as the reason for the household advice
theories.boringExplanation: The PHP flaws are real and are being exploited, and the UK minister did cite cyberattacks. But the flaws affect web servers, not grid control systems, and no official has connected them to the preparedness advice. Patch orders with three-day deadlines are routine for critical flaws.

theories.title: Preparation for a renewed war with Iran after the midterms
theories.trigger: A decision to resume strikes, with planners expecting retaliation against infrastructure, including cyber and drone attacks on the homeland.
earlySigns: Carrier and air-defense movements reported by multiple outlets
Evacuation advisories for US citizens in the region
Congressional briefings or war-powers notices
theories.boringExplanation: Strikes near Hormuz on the eve of the vote are a real escalation sign and the one theory on this board with new evidence. What is still missing: any official linking the base plan or the household advice to Iran, and any completion date for FORTRESS that would fit a short timeline.

theories.title: Europe stocking up because war with Russia is close
theories.trigger: Intelligence that Russia is preparing a move against a NATO member, with hybrid attacks on power, water and transport expected first.
earlySigns: Troop concentrations and mobilization reported by allied governments
Reserve call-ups in frontline states
Civil defense drills with dates, not leaflets
theories.boringExplanation: Streeting's 1,000-days line is a budget and readiness argument, and Europe's household guidance has been building since the EU's March 2025 strategy. Guidance ranging from 3 days to 2 weeks across countries looks like each government picking a number, not a shared alarm.

theories.title: Hardening bases for a conflict with China over Taiwan
theories.trigger: Planners expecting that a Pacific war would begin with attacks on US power and logistics at home, so bases need to run alone for months.
earlySigns: Pacific base construction and prepositioning in budget documents
Taiwan Strait incidents reported by wire services
Export controls and sanctions tightening in the same weeks
theories.boringExplanation: FORTRESS reads like a long-horizon program, which is what a China planner would write, but also what any planner would write after a year of grid attacks. Nothing on the board ties the timing to the Pacific.

theories.title: A Carrington-class solar storm
theories.trigger: A large coronal mass ejection aimed at Earth. In 1859 the Carrington event set telegraph lines sparking and lit auroras near the equator. On today's grid it could damage large transformers that take months to replace.
earlySigns: A NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center watch, which gives one to three days of notice
Grid operators announcing protective shutdowns
Nobody can schedule it, so a date like November 17 would be a coincidence
theories.boringExplanation: Nobody notable is pushing this in October 2026 and no space-weather watch is in effect. It appears here because it is the one scenario where 90 days of base self-sufficiency makes plain sense, and because a 2024 Simpsons solar-storm claim was already debunked.

theories.title: Something happens around the November 3 midterms
theories.trigger: A plan to disrupt or delay the election, or an expectation of unrest after it, with the preparedness advice as cover.
earlySigns: State election officials reporting threats or interference
National Guard activations announced before the vote
Officials refusing to commit to a normal count
theories.boringExplanation: The vote has now passed. Democrats won both chambers, election day had no major cyber or grid incident, and nothing was revealed afterward. The alert test two weeks later was scheduled in September under a law that requires one every three years.

theories.title: A staged attack on the grid, then water
theories.trigger: A government deciding to manufacture a crisis. This would require thousands of people to keep a secret and would leave a paper trail in the agencies told to prepare.
earlySigns: Leaks from people inside those agencies
Preparations that only make sense if the date is known in advance
Media pre-positioned on a story before it breaks
theories.boringExplanation: Every item pointing at this is a social post with no source beyond itself. The Simpsons episode people cite aired in 2023 and shows no date. The same November 17 claim circulated in 2025 and nothing happened.

nov17.title: What November 17 actually is
nov17.text: FEMA and the FCC scheduled a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System for Tuesday, November 17, 2026, between 2:20 and 2:50 pm Eastern, with December 3 as the backup date. It goes to radio, TV, cable and satellite. Phones are not part of this one. Federal law requires a national test at least every three years, and earlier ones ran in 2011, 2017, 2018 and 2023. FEMA calls it routine and no official source links it to FORTRESS. A claim that a worldwide 72-hour blackout will happen that day is a hoax that fact-checkers rated false.
